malva-parviflora.summary: Cheeseweed mallow gets its name from its round, segmented fruits, which look like tiny wheels of cheese. This annual herb grows in gardens, cultivated ground and other disturbed places, with rounded, shallowly lobed leaves and small pale flowers tucked beside the leaf stalks. Its deep taproot becomes woody as the plant matures. Seeds have tough coats and can remain in the soil, so removing young plants before they fruit is much easier than tackling an established patch.

rosa-laevigata.summary: Cherokee rose is a vigorous scrambling shrub whose long, hooked canes climb through nearby vegetation. Large white flowers with golden centers stand out against glossy leaves, usually divided into three leaflets; bristly orange-red hips follow. Despite its common name, the plant is native to parts of Asia and was brought to North America during colonial times. It can spread aggressively in the southeastern United States, where a locally native climbing plant is often a better garden choice.

enarmonia-formosana.summary: Cherry bark tortrix is a small, intricately patterned moth whose caterpillars live beneath tree bark. Cherries, plums, apples and other members of the rose family can serve as hosts. Eggs are laid on bark, often near wounds, and the larvae tunnel below the surface, causing cracking and sometimes conspicuous gum. The insect is established in parts of the Pacific Northwest. An adult moth may be easy to overlook; damaged bark near the base of a tree can be the first useful clue.

prunus-laurocerasus.summary: Cherry laurel is a dense evergreen shrub or small tree with broad, glossy leaves and upright clusters of fragrant white flowers. Its dark fruits attract birds, which carry the seeds beyond planted hedges. In the Puget Sound region, escaped plants can thrive in forest shade and crowd native shrubs and tree seedlings. Branches touching the ground can also take root. Cutting a large plant once seldom finishes the job, because both roots and cut stems can produce new growth.

prunus-cerasifera.summary: Cherry plum is a small deciduous tree that flowers early, often as its first leaves unfold. The species has green leaves and white blossoms, although familiar garden cultivars may have deep purple foliage and pink flowers. Small, smooth-skinned plums range from yellow to red and attract birds. Native to southeastern Europe and parts of Asia, it has escaped cultivation in several regions, including parts of the United States and southeastern Australia. A purple leaf alone identifies neither the species nor its local ecological impact.

cryphonectria-parasitica.summary: Chestnut blight is caused by a fungus that grows in the bark of chestnut trees. Infection can expand around a branch or trunk, interrupting its supply of water and nutrients and leaving wilted brown leaves above the damaged area. Sunken or cracked cankers may carry tiny orange fruiting bodies. The disease transformed eastern North American forests by devastating American chestnut. It also affects European sweet chestnut; ongoing breeding work seeks useful resistance, but an apparently healthy tree is not proof of lasting protection.

gnomoniopsis-smithogilvyi.summary: Chestnut brown rot can hide inside a nut that looks ordinary from the outside. This fungus damages chestnut kernels, which may become brown, chalky or sponge-like, reducing the quality of the harvest. It can also live in apparently healthy flowers and shoots, and has been associated with twig cankers. Research in Portugal confirmed that isolates caused disease in several sweet-chestnut varieties. Because other fungi produce similar symptoms, a cut nut or bark lesion is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable identification on its own.

sphenoclea-zeylanica.summary: Chickenspike is an annual wetland herb with soft, upright stems and narrow flower spikes that rise above its leaves. The tiny white flowers are packed closely together, followed by small capsules containing numerous seeds. It grows in shallow water, ditches and flooded ground, and is familiar as a rice-field weed. Its native range spans tropical Africa, Asia and northern Australia. The fleshy lower stem and dense, tapering flower spike are useful clues when examining a plant at the water's edge.

astragalus-cicer.summary: Chickpea milkvetch, also called cicer milkvetch, is a long-lived perennial legume grown for forage and soil stabilization. Its leafy stems carry many paired leaflets and clusters of pale yellow to white pea flowers. The inflated pods darken as they mature, and loose seeds may rattle inside. Native to Europe and the Caucasus region, it spreads through underground shoots as well as seed. Its agricultural usefulness is well documented; its presence in this catalog should not be read as proof that it is invasive everywhere.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online

cichorium-intybus.summary: Chicory brings clear blue flowers to many roadsides and old fields, opening its flower heads along stiff, branching stems. Young plants begin as a rosette of leaves that can resemble a dandelion, above a substantial taproot with milky sap. This Eurasian plant has a long history of cultivation for leaves and roots, and is now naturalized widely in North America. Wild chicory favors disturbed ground and usually does not move far into undisturbed habitats. Its flowers often close around midday.

oenothera-stricta.summary: Chilean evening primrose opens yellow flowers that take on orange or reddish tones as they age. It begins with a rosette of narrow leaves, then sends up a leafy flowering stem from a stout taproot. Usually annual or biennial, it comes from Chile and Argentina and has naturalized in disturbed places beyond that range. Flowers open toward evening and may remain open into the following day. The long floral tube and slender, upright seed capsules help distinguish it from other yellow-flowered plants.

gunnera-tinctoria.summary: Chilean gunnera makes a striking clump of enormous, rough-edged leaves on stout, prickly stalks. Despite the nickname giant rhubarb, it is not culinary rhubarb. Its leaves die back seasonally, leaving large buds on thick rhizomes ready for new growth. In invaded areas of Ireland it forms dense colonies in wet ground, along waterways and on coastal sites, shading smaller plants. Other large gunneras, including garden hybrids, can look similar, so the familiar umbrella-shaped leaf is only the beginning of an identification.

sources.label: Northern Ireland Environment Agency species account

cestrum-parqui.summary: Chilean jessamine is a woody shrub with narrow, glossy leaves and clusters of slender yellow-green flowers. Dark, egg-shaped berries follow the blooms, and birds or water can carry them away from the parent plant. It often grows along disturbed ground and waterways in regions where it has escaped gardens. This plant is particularly troublesome around livestock because its leaves and berries are poisonous, and cut or wilted material remains hazardous. Its soft green stems can develop into a substantial, persistent shrub.

loxosceles-laeta.summary: The Chilean recluse is a brown spider native to South America that has also been introduced elsewhere. It favors sheltered spaces, and established populations outside its native range are sometimes confined to buildings. Its body and legs may be yellowish, reddish brown or darker, with a violin-like marking that can be less obvious than that of the familiar brown recluse. Reliable separation from related recluses requires closer examination than color alone. In quiet corners, its web and secretive habits can make it easy to miss.

melia-azedarach.summary: Chinaberry is a deciduous tree with a spreading crown, finely divided leaves and fragrant lilac-colored flowers. Yellowish fruits often remain on bare branches through winter, making the tree conspicuous after leaf fall. Native across parts of Asia and Australia, it was widely planted for shade and ornament. It now grows along roads, fields and forest openings in the southeastern United States, where it can spread aggressively. The attractive fruits are poisonous and should not be mistaken for something to eat.

ficus-microcarpa.summary: Chinese banyan can begin life perched on another tree, then develop into a broad evergreen with hanging aerial roots. Some of those roots reach the ground and become pillar-like supports. Its smooth gray bark, leathery leaves and small rounded figs are familiar features of warm-climate plantings. The species is also widely grown as a houseplant and bonsai. Seed production depends on a tiny associated fig wasp, so the arrival of a pollinator can change how a cultivated tree reproduces outside its original range.

catalpa-ovata.summary: Chinese catalpa is a deciduous tree with broad, often three-lobed leaves and airy clusters of pale yellow flowers. Purple markings decorate the flowers, which are smaller than those of the two familiar American catalpas. Long, narrow seed capsules follow and can resemble green beans while young. Native to China, the tree has been cultivated well beyond its home range and sometimes self-sows in the United States. Its large leaves and hanging capsules give it a distinctive appearance even when the flowers are gone.

cunninghamia-lanceolata.summary: Chinese fir is an evergreen conifer with a tall, tapering crown and spreading branches whose tips often droop. Its stiff, pointed leaves sit closely along the shoots, giving the foliage a flattened, layered look. Small cones mature from green to brown, while older bark breaks into flakes that reveal warmer reddish tones beneath. Native to China, it is grown as an ornamental tree elsewhere. Old brown foliage may stay attached for years, so interior browning is not by itself evidence of a new disease.

pyracantha-fortuneana.summary: Chinese firethorn is a spiny shrub grown for its clusters of white flowers and bright red fruits. Its leaves are broadest toward the tip, with rounded or slightly notched ends and small teeth along the edges. Plants cultivated under this name have occasionally naturalized in Australia. The name itself needs care: some floras retain Pyracantha fortuneana, while Kew currently places it within P. crenulata. That disagreement matters when comparing photographs, records or management advice published under different firethorn names.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online

koelreuteria-elegans.summary: Chinese flame tree is grown for bright yellow flowers and colorful, papery seed capsules. The Taiwanese form, subspecies formosana, has large, twice-divided leaves and three-sided capsules that turn from red or pink to brown as they mature. That ornamental form has escaped in southeastern Queensland and northeastern New South Wales, where it is treated as an environmental weed. The species also includes a Fijian subspecies, so accounts of the Taiwanese garden tree should not automatically be applied to every population.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online

celtis-sinensis.summary: Chinese hackberry is a fast-growing deciduous tree with smooth gray bark and a broad, spreading crown. Its glossy leaves have teeth mostly toward their tips, and small round fruits ripen through orange and red. Birds help carry its seeds away from planted trees. In parts of eastern Australia, dense stands form along creeks and disturbed forest openings, preventing native vegetation from regenerating. The tree is native to eastern Asia, and its local behavior depends on climate and setting.

holmskioldia-sanguinea.summary: Chinese hatplant is a scrambling woody shrub named for the small, colorful saucers around its flowers. A curved red flower tube emerges from each broad orange-red calyx, creating the hat-like outline. Oval leaves grow along the loose, climbing stems. Native from the Himalayan region toward Myanmar, it is grown as an ornamental in warm climates and can be trained over a support. The showy calyx is part of the flower's outer structure, rather than a flat petal.

cynoglossum-amabile.summary: Chinese hound's tongue is often sold as Chinese forget-me-not for its sprays of small sky-blue flowers. The plant is bushy, with softly hairy, gray-green leaves, and may behave as an annual or biennial depending on the climate. Garden selections also have white or pink flowers. It can flower in its first year and reseed freely, which explains why it sometimes appears beyond its intended bed. It favors cooler growing conditions and may lose vigor during long, hot summers.

eragrostis-unioloides.summary: Chinese lovegrass is a small tuft-forming grass whose open seed heads carry flattened clusters of tiny flowers. These spikelets can turn purplish red as they mature, giving the airy heads a subtle wash of color. Its stems may rise from a leaning base, and plants grow as annuals or short-lived perennials. Native across tropical and subtropical Asia into parts of Queensland, it occurs in grasslands and along roadsides. Similar lovegrasses are difficult to separate, so close views of mature spikelets are more useful than a distant photograph.

sources.label: Kew GrassBase and Flora of Oman

tenodera-sinensis.summary: Chinese mantis is a large, slender hunter that waits among leaves and stems with its grasping forelegs folded. Adults range from green to tan or brown, often with a green line along the wings. The head swivels to follow nearby movement. Introduced to North America, it feeds on a broad range of animals it can overpower, including other beneficial insects. Its rounded, foam-like egg case remains on twigs after the adult season and can be mistaken for a small brown growth on the plant.

eriocheir-sinensis.summary: Chinese mitten crab is named for the dense bristles that cover its claws like fuzzy gloves. It spends much of its life in rivers and other freshwater habitats, then moves toward saltier water to reproduce. Originally from coastal China and Korea, it has been carried to other regions through human activity. Where abundant, its burrows can undermine banks, and its feeding and migrations can interfere with native wildlife and fisheries. Small juveniles may lack the obvious hairy claws seen on adults.

sources.label: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

cipangopaludina-chinensis.summary: Chinese mysterysnails carry a rounded olive-brown shell with deep seams between its coils and a hard door that closes the opening. These freshwater snails graze on algae and decaying material in ponds, lakes and slow-moving water. Females give birth to live young, a feature behind the 'mystery' name. Introduced from Asia through human transport, they can move again with aquarium releases or aquatic equipment. Keep unwanted snails out of waterways and check boats and gear before leaving the water.

parlatoreopsis-chinensis.summary: Chinese obscure scale is a tiny armored insect found on woody plants, including crabapple. Females live beneath protective covers, and their identity usually depends on microscopic examination. Historical observations in Missouri describe overlapping generations and fertilized females surviving winter. A Korean import study also found the species on a tree brought from China, showing why nursery inspections matter. Older accounts sometimes confused it with a related scale, so an extension diagnosis is a better starting point than treating every crust-like patch on a branch as this species.

sources.label: Korean Journal of Applied Entomology import-interception study

firmiana-simplex.summary: Chinese parasoltree has an unusual green trunk and large, lobed leaves that cast a broad patch of shade. This fast-growing deciduous tree carries loose clusters of small pale flowers, followed by distinctive pods and round seeds. Leaves turn yellow before falling, leaving the green bark especially noticeable in winter. Long cultivated outside eastern Asia, it can produce abundant seedlings and has become invasive in several southeastern states. The seedlings around a mature planting are often the clearest sign that it is spreading.

stranvaesia-davidiana.summary: Chinese photinia is an evergreen shrub or small tree whose clusters of red fruits can brighten the branches well into winter. Small white flowers precede the fruit, and its narrow leaves may have gently wavy edges. It comes from China and nearby parts of Asia, where it grows on slopes, in thickets and along riverbanks. Gardeners also know it as Photinia davidiana. The two names refer to the same plant in the accounts used here, rather than to two different red-berried shrubs.

ligustrum-sinense.summary: Chinese privet is a densely branching shrub that often keeps its small leaves through winter in mild climates. Clusters of white flowers are followed by dark fruits that birds and mammals carry into new places. Introduced as an ornamental, it has become a major invader in parts of the eastern and southern United States. Seeds and root suckers both help it form thickets, which can replace a more varied layer of native plants. An old hedge can therefore be a continuing source of new plants beyond the garden.

gonocarpus-chinensis.summary: Chinese raspwort is a small perennial of wet tropical regions, native from southern China through parts of Southeast Asia and the Pacific to Australia. It is easy to overlook beside larger wetland plants. The New South Wales form has rough, four-ribbed stems, narrow toothed leaves and tiny flowers followed by ribbed fruits. Its Australian subspecies is treated separately in this collection, so a close look at the fruit matters when putting a precise name to a plant.

gonocarpus-chinensis-ssp-verrucosus.summary: This Australian subspecies of Chinese raspwort is a slender perennial of damp, open ground. Its small toothed leaves sit mostly in opposite pairs on rough, four-ribbed stems, and the flowers are tiny enough to need a close look. The rounded fruits carry eight ribs, small bumps and short curved hairs, useful details for a careful identification. Native to eastern Australia, it has also been introduced to California and Hawaii; that history alone does not establish how it affects a particular wetland.

lepadoretus-sinicus.summary: Chinese rose beetles often reveal themselves through the lace-like holes they leave between leaf veins. Adults emerge after dusk to feed on many kinds of plants, including garden ornamentals and crops. They are small brown scarabs covered with pale hairs, while their whitish grubs develop underground. The beetle is usually called Adoretus sinicus in modern identification guides. Because a close relative looks almost identical, feeding damage and a photograph can suggest an identification but may not settle it.

miscanthus-sinensis.summary: Chinese silvergrass forms tall, arching clumps topped by airy flower plumes. Familiar from ornamental plantings, this Asian perennial can send windborne seeds beyond the garden and establish along roadsides and other disturbed ground. Older clumps develop a substantial underground mass that makes removal difficult. Cultivars differ in size, leaf pattern and fertility, so a garden label is worth keeping, but it does not replace checking for seedlings nearby. In regions where it spreads, a locally appropriate native grass is a better planting choice.

triadica-sebifera.summary: Chinese tallow is often noticed for its autumn color and clusters of white seeds that resemble popcorn. The deciduous tree has broadly rounded leaves drawn out into slender tips and produces yellow flower spikes in spring. Brought from Asia as an ornamental and potential crop, it now invades wetlands, prairies and forests in the southeastern United States. Birds and water carry its seeds, while cut trees can sprout again. Removing seedlings early and planning follow-up for larger trees helps prevent a return.

asystasia-gangetica.summary: Chinese violet is a creeping perennial with opposite leaves, trumpet-shaped flowers and seed capsules that spring open when ripe. Garden forms can spread quickly in warm climates. The name covers more than one subspecies: the small white flowers with purple markings belong to subsp. micrantha, a serious smothering weed in parts of Australia, while other forms have larger, differently colored flowers. Stems can root where they touch moist soil, making dumped cuttings an effective way to start a new patch.

wisteria-sinensis.summary: Chinese wisteria's fragrant spring flower clusters can be beautiful, but the woody vine grows with enough force to overwhelm trees and shrubs. It climbs by twining and can also spread across the ground, where touching stems take root. The hanging seed pods are velvety, unlike those of native American wisteria. Escaped vines can shade woodland plants and tighten around their supports. Successful removal usually takes follow-up because cutting an established vine commonly produces fresh shoots.

dioscorea-oppositifolia.summary: Dioscorea oppositifolia is a tuber-forming climbing yam native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar. Its name has often been applied incorrectly to Chinese yam in North American writing. That distinction matters: descriptions of the invasive Chinese yam cannot simply be transferred to this species. This record needs its scientific name and intended common name reconciled before a reliable field guide or removal recommendation can be attached to it.

rorippa-cantoniensis.summary: Chinese yellowcress is a small annual mustard native to eastern Asia. Its lower leaves are divided into lobes, while the smaller leaves higher on the stem clasp it at their bases. Small flowers give way to short, slender cylindrical seed pods. A close look is worthwhile because several yellowcresses share this modest appearance, and leaf shape changes as the plant grows. Photographs showing both the low leaves and mature pods are much more useful than a single flower portrait.

pinus-roxburghii.summary: Chir pine is a tall Himalayan pine with notably long needles carried in bundles of three. Its elongated, egg-shaped woody cones are another useful feature, especially when compared with the shorter cones of some familiar landscape pines. Native from Pakistan through the Himalaya and northern India, it has long been valued as a source of resin. A planted tree is not by itself evidence of an invasion; seedlings growing beyond cultivation deserve a separate, locally informed assessment.

ephestia-elutella.summary: The chocolate moth, also called the cacao or tobacco moth, is a small moth associated with stored goods. Its larvae feed in products such as cocoa, tobacco, cereals and dried foods, so an indoor sighting is a reason to inspect supplies rather than assume the moth came from the garden. Adults have a wingspan of roughly 15-20 millimeters and resemble several related warehouse moths. Warm storage conditions allow populations to develop more quickly, and a precise identification may require an expert.

akebia-quinata.summary: Chocolate vine has five smooth leaflets arranged like the fingers of a hand and small, dark, fragrant flowers in spring. This woody climber comes from eastern Asia and can grow rapidly over shrubs and other vegetation. Its unusual purple fruits may split open to reveal pale pulp and dark seeds, which birds can carry elsewhere. In mild climates it keeps much of its foliage through winter. Once established, repeated pruning may not be enough to contain it, making early attention to escapes worthwhile.

melochia-corchorifolia.summary: Chocolateweed is a small upright herb or subshrub with toothed leaves and tight clusters of little flowers. Despite its common name, the flowers may be white, pink or purple, with regional variation described in botanical floras. Rounded, hairy capsules follow the blooms. The plant occurs widely across warm parts of the Old World and Australia, including damp or seasonally wet places. Its name should not be taken as proof that every population is unwanted: it is native in parts of its range.

sources.label: Kew hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa

leonotis-nepetifolia.summary: Christmas candlestick stands out for the rounded clusters of orange flowers spaced along its upright stems. Also called lion's tail, it has opposite toothed leaves and can grow taller than a person in warm conditions. Botanical accounts place its native range in Africa and the Indian subcontinent. Introduced populations can form large colonies; a Queensland management account describes displacement of native vegetation along riverbanks and floodplains. Seeds can travel in water or muddy equipment, so keeping them on site matters during removal.

sources.label: Kew hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa

themeda-arguens.summary: Christmas grass is a tufted tropical grass whose seed heads reward a closer look. Small groups of spikelets sit within papery bracts, and each fertile unit carries a conspicuous bent, twisted bristle. Most leaves arise near the base of the plant. Native across parts of tropical Asia to northern Australia, it belongs to the same genus as other grasses that can look similar from a distance. Mature flowering material is therefore much more useful for identification than a photograph of the leaves alone.

macrosiphoniella-sanborni.summary: Chrysanthemum aphids gather around tender shoots, buds and leaf undersides, where they feed on plant sap. The small adults are dark reddish brown to nearly black; younger aphids are often dull brick red. Colonies can build quickly because females give birth to live young, and infested plants can carry them between greenhouses. Feeding may distort or stunt growth, while sticky honeydew supports black sooty mold. Regularly checking new shoots and incoming plants helps catch a colony before it becomes dense.

sources.label: NC State AG-136 via University of Minnesota

lasioderma-serricorne.summary: Cigarette beetles are tiny, rounded, reddish-brown insects that can turn up in far more than tobacco. Their larvae feed in dried products, including spices, grains, pet food and other stored plant material. The adult's head is tucked beneath its thorax, giving it a hooded appearance from above. Fine details help separate it from the similar drugstore beetle: cigarette beetles have saw-toothed antennae and lack rows of pits on their wing covers. Finding the infested material is more useful than treating a wandering adult.

cinnamomum-verum.summary: True cinnamon is the Sri Lankan tree whose bark supplies the familiar spice. Fresh leaves often emerge red before turning glossy green, and several strong veins run from near the leaf base toward the tip. Small pale flowers are followed by dark, fleshy, single-seeded fruits. In tropical gardens the tree can become a substantial evergreen. Because other cinnamon relatives share aromatic leaves and bark, a scent alone is a poor identification test; leaf arrangement, veins and fruit provide a better starting point.

sources.label: Kew hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa

dynaspidiotus-tsugae.summary: Circular hemlock scale is a tiny armored insect that settles mainly beneath conifer needles. Females sit under rounded, dark brown covers with a raised center; heavy infestations can coat much of a needle. Feeding removes plant fluids and may lead to yellowing and premature needle loss, particularly on hemlocks. Also called shortneedle evergreen scale, it has a mobile crawler stage before the insects settle. Inspecting the lower crown with a hand lens can reveal a problem before thinning foliage becomes obvious.
